{{more footnotes|date=August 2021}}
In [[set theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], an '''additively indecomposable ordinal''' ''&alpha;'' is any [[ordinal number]] that is not 0 such that for any  <math>\beta,\gamma<\alpha</math>, we have  <math>\beta+\gamma<\alpha.</math>  Additively indecomposable ordinals were named the ''gamma numbers'' by [[Georg Cantor|Cantor]],<ref name="Rhea2017">A. Rhea, "[https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08908 The Ordinals as a Consummate Abstraction of Number Systems]" (2017), preprint.</ref><sup>p.20</sup> and are also called ''additive principal numbers''.  The [[class (set theory)|class]] of additively indecomposable ordinals may be denoted <math>\mathbb H</math>, from the German "Hauptzahl".<ref>W. Pohlers, "A short course in ordinal analysis", pp. 27–78. Appearing in [[Peter Aczel|Aczel]], Simmons, ''Proof Theory: A selection of papers from the Leeds Proof Theory Programme 1990'' (1992). Cambridge University Press, {{ISBN|978-0-521-41413-5}}</ref>  The additively indecomposable ordinals are precisely those ordinals of the form <math>\omega^\beta</math> for some ordinal <math>\beta</math>.

From the [[Continuous function (set theory)|continuity]] of addition in its right argument, we get that if <math>\beta < \alpha</math> and ''&alpha;'' is additively indecomposable, then <math>\beta + \alpha = \alpha.</math>

Obviously  1 is additively indecomposable, since <math>0+0<1.</math> No [[finite set|finite]] ordinal other than <math>1</math> is additively indecomposable. Also,  <math>\omega</math> is additively indecomposable, since the sum of two finite ordinals is still finite. More generally, every [[infinite set|infinite]] [[initial ordinal]] (an ordinal corresponding to a [[cardinal number]]) is additively indecomposable.

The class of additively indecomposable numbers  is [[Order topology|closed]] and unbounded. Its enumerating function  is [[normal function|normal]], given by <math>\omega^\alpha</math>.

The derivative  of <math>\omega^\alpha</math> (which enumerates its fixed points) is written  <math>\varepsilon_\alpha</math> Ordinals of this form (that is, [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]]s of <math>\omega^\alpha</math>) are called ''[[epsilon numbers (mathematics)|epsilon numbers]]''. The number  <math>\varepsilon_0 = \omega^{\omega^{\omega^{\cdots}}}</math> is therefore the first fixed point of the [[sequence]]  <math>\omega,\omega^\omega\!,\omega^{\omega^\omega}\!\!,\ldots</math>

== Multiplicatively indecomposable ==
A similar notion can be defined for multiplication. If ''&alpha;'' is greater than the multiplicative identity, 1, and ''&beta;'' < ''&alpha;'' and ''&gamma;'' < ''&alpha;'' imply ''&beta;''·''&gamma;'' < ''&alpha;'', then ''&alpha;'' is multiplicatively indecomposable. The finite ordinal 2 is multiplicatively indecomposable since 1·1 = 1 < 2. Besides 2, the multiplicatively indecomposable ordinals (named the ''delta numbers'' by Cantor<ref name="Rhea2017" /><sup>p.20</sup>) are those of the form <math>\omega^{\omega^\alpha} \,</math> for any ordinal ''&alpha;''. Every [[Epsilon numbers (mathematics)|epsilon number]] is multiplicatively indecomposable; and every multiplicatively indecomposable ordinal (other than 2) is additively indecomposable. The delta numbers (other than 2) are the same as the [[prime ordinal]]s that are limits.

== Higher indecomposables ==
Exponentially indecomposable ordinals are equal to the epsilon numbers.
Tetration, as usually defined, gets stuck at limit ordinals, so the notion of indecomposable beyond exponentiation is not useful.
